text: Hosts hand guests a pair of spare house slippers as soon as they take their shoes off.
note: Spare guest slippers are standard in many Polish, Ukrainian, Turkish and Korean homes; walking around in socks feels a bit odd.

text: Your name day gets celebrated by family and colleagues almost like a second birthday.
note: Imieniny: Poles celebrate the saint's day that matches their first name, and calendars print the names for each day.

text: Saying "thank you" as you hand cash to a waiter can mean "keep the change".
note: 'Dziękuję' while paying often tells the waiter to keep the rest, so wait until you have your change before thanking them.

text: Most big shops are closed on Sundays, so Saturday is the busy shopping day.
note: Poland has banned most Sunday trading since 2018; in France most shops close on Sundays too, apart from bakeries, markets and tourist areas.

text: A "second breakfast" around 11 am is a normal part of school and office life.
note: 'Drugie śniadanie' is a sandwich or fruit packed for mid-morning; kids take it to school in a lunchbox.

text: Opening a window on a hot bus can start an argument, because a draught is said to make you ill.
note: Draughts get blamed for colds and stiff necks: 'przeciąg' in Poland, 'protiah' in Ukraine, 'colpo d'aria' in Italy, 'cereyan' in Türkiye.

text: Weekend mushroom picking in the forest is a beloved hobby, and the best spots are kept secret.
note: Polish 'grzybobranie', Ukrainian 'quiet hunting', Italian porcini and French cèpes: foragers know which species are safe and guard their spots.

text: Older gentlemen may greet a woman by kissing her hand.
note: Hand-kissing ('całowanie w rękę') survives mostly among older men and at formal events; younger people see it as old-fashioned.

text: Hosts set out a full table and modestly call it "whatever the cottage has".
note: 'Czym chata bogata' (what the cottage is rich in) is a humble way of saying 'help yourself to everything we have'.

text: A quick visit "for coffee" easily turns into soup, a main course and cake.
note: Afternoon visits often overlap with the main hot meal ('obiad' in Poland, 'obid' in Ukraine), and hosts rarely let a guest leave without eating.

text: When guests leave, the host packs them leftovers "for the road".
note: Sending food home is part of hospitality. Mexicans even have a word for the parcel, 'itacate'; Italian hosts wrap up a 'pacchettino'.

text: At birthdays, everyone sings a song wishing the person a hundred years of life.
note: 'Sto lat' (a hundred years) is also sung at weddings, sports wins and retirements. Some add: 'two hundred!'

text: At the big winter holiday dinner, one extra place is set for an unexpected guest.
note: Christmas Eve dinner ('Wigilia' in Poland, 'Sviatvechir' in Ukraine): the empty place welcomes a traveller or anyone alone, and tradition calls for 12 dishes.
comments: UA added in review; note updated

text: On the first day of spring, kids throw a straw doll into a river to say goodbye to winter.
note: Marzanna, a straw figure of winter, is drowned or burned around 21 March; school classes still march her to the river.

text: On the Monday after Easter, people soak each other with buckets and water pistols.
note: Poland's 'Śmigus-dyngus' and western Ukraine's 'Oblyvanyi ponedilok' (Doused Monday): getting drenched is said to bring luck.

text: On one Thursday in late winter, people queue at bakeries and eat doughnuts all day.
note: 'Tłusty czwartek' (Fat Thursday) comes before Lent; eating at least one 'pączek' is said to bring luck for the year.

text: Asked how you are, a small complaint is the normal answer; "great!" can sound like boasting.
note: Grumbling is a bonding ritual. 'Could be worse' or 'getting by' are standard replies, and 'great!' can tempt fate.
comments: I corrected the [note] since it’s relevant for PL and UA

text: The classic TV comedy is a cabaret troupe doing sketches and songs, more than stand-up.
note: Kabaret troupes fill holiday TV schedules and tour the country; stand-up became popular only more recently.

text: The cheeky boy in classic school jokes is called Johnny.
note: Polish 'Jasio' is the English 'Little Johnny', the Dutch 'Jantje' and the Brazilian 'Joãozinho'. Italy's version is Pierino, France's Toto.

text: Strangers rarely smile at each other on the street; a big grin at a stranger can seem odd.
note: Smiles are kept for people you know. A serious face in public is neutral, not unfriendly.

text: "Not my circus, not my monkeys" is a common way of saying "not my problem".
note: 'Nie mój cyrk, nie moje małpy' has spread into English online, but it started as a Polish saying.

text: A polite but warm way to address someone is "Mrs" or "Mr" plus their first name, like "Mrs Anna".
note: 'Pani Anno', 'Panie Tomku': formal Pan/Pani with a first name sits between strict politeness and first-name terms.

text: Something very easy is "a bread roll with butter".
note: 'Bułka z masłem' is the local 'piece of cake'.

text: Facing a messy plan, people shrug and say "somehow it will be".
note: 'Jakoś to będzie' is both a joke about improvising at the last minute and a sincere coping motto.

text: At work, moving to first-name terms is offered by the older or more senior person, never assumed.
note: Switching to the informal 'you' is a small ritual. Until then it stays formal.
comments: I removed mentioning of different countries from {note}

text: In early May, offices go quiet as people bridge two public holidays into a long break.
note: 'Majówka': 1 and 3 May are holidays, so taking 2 May off makes a mini-vacation, often with the first barbecue of the year.

text: A boss or doctor is addressed by their title, like "Mr Director" or "Mrs Doctor".
note: Titles show respect: 'Panie Dyrektorze' in Poland, 'Dottore' in Italy, 'Licenciado' or 'Ingeniero' in Mexico.

text: In casual chat, the word "no" actually means "yeah".
note: 'No' is a colloquial 'yeah' among friends ('no tak' = yes, sure); the real 'no' is 'nie'. Stick to 'tak' in formal settings.

text: Emails asking for a favour end with "thank you from the mountain".
note: 'Z góry dziękuję': 'z góry' means both 'from the top' and 'in advance', so it's simply 'thanks in advance'.

text: A daydreamer is said to be "thinking about blue almonds".
note: 'Myśleć o niebieskich migdałach'. Someone newly in love is 'floating in the clouds'.

text: An off-topic remark gets the reply "what does gingerbread have to do with a windmill?"
note: 'Co ma piernik do wiatraka?' means 'how is that relevant?'

text: The highest praise for a loyal friend: "you could steal horses with them".
note: 'Można z nim konie kraść': a trustworthy, up-for-anything person.

text: The middle of nowhere is "where the devil says goodnight".
note: 'Gdzie diabeł mówi dobranoc': a remote place that's hard to reach.

text: Kids who keep nagging are told to stop "drilling a hole in my belly".
note: 'Przestań mi wiercić dziurę w brzuchu' means 'stop pestering me', a phrase every child hears.

text: Any pair of trainers gets called by one sports brand's name, whatever the logo.
note: 'Adidasy' is the everyday word for sneakers, the way some people say 'hoover' for any vacuum cleaner.

text: Christmas doesn't feel complete until the 1990 film about a boy left home alone is on TV.
note: In Poland ('Kevin sam w domu') and Ukraine ('Sam udoma') it airs every holiday season; when a Polish channel dropped it in 2010, viewers protested.
comments: UA added in review; note updated

text: On 30 September, girls give the boys in class small gifts, and offices treat the men.
note: 'Dzień Chłopaka' (Boys' Day) is the informal counterpart to Women's Day: sweets, cards and a bit of teasing.

text: In late January, kindergartens put on shows for the children's grandmas and grandpas.
note: 'Dzień Babci' (21 January) and 'Dzień Dziadka' (22 January): kids make cards and perform songs and poems.

text: About 100 days before their final school exams, students hold a ball that opens with a stately group dance.
note: 'Studniówka' comes from 'sto' (a hundred); the opening polonaise is rehearsed for weeks.

text: On the night of 29 November, friends pour hot wax through a key into water to read the future.
note: St Andrew's Eve: Poles call it 'Andrzejki', Ukrainians 'Andriivski vechornytsi'. The wax shadow once predicted a husband; now it's a party game.

text: University lectures traditionally start 15 minutes late, and nobody minds.
note: The 'kwadrans akademicki' (academic quarter) is tolerated for lecturers, less so for students.

text: On Sundays, many convenience stores stay open by also working as a post office.
note: The 2018 Sunday trading ban exempts postal outlets, so a big chain added parcel services. Lawmakers have tried to close the loophole.

text: Students turn up to big exams in a white shirt and dark trousers or skirt.
note: The 'strój galowy' (gala outfit) is also worn for school ceremonies and the start of the school year.

text: An old story someone keeps bringing back is a "reheated cutlet".
note: 'Odgrzewany kotlet': a rehashed topic or a stale joke.

text: Saying it bluntly is speaking "straight from the bridge".
note: 'Mówić prosto z mostu': to say it frankly, without beating around the bush.

text: To pay or take out cash, you type a six-digit code from your banking app into the terminal or ATM, no card needed.
note: BLIK codes work in shops, online checkouts and cash machines; each code expires within minutes. It's a home-grown system, rarely seen abroad.

text: For a colleague's leaving gift or a friend's trip, someone sets up an online pot and the link goes round the group chat for small contributions.
note: Polish 'zrzutka' (a crowdfunding site of that name is used mostly for private collections); Brazilian 'vaquinha'; Ukrainian 'skynutysia'.
comments: fits guess for BR UA NL

text: Online orders are collected from a metal parcel locker near your block, which opens with a code on your phone.
note: Poland's InPost 'paczkomaty' stand at shops, stations and housing estates, open 24/7; Ukraine and the Netherlands also run locker networks.

text: Leaving your parents' home, you get a bag of jars: pickles, jam, soup, compote.
note: Parents send grown-up kids back to the city with home cooking in jars, and the empty jars are expected back on the next visit.
comments: UA and KR fits from general knowledge; slang is derogatory, keep only in note

text: The housewarming party is nicknamed after the window ledge, where the first snacks were put.
note: 'Parapetówka' comes from 'parapet' (window ledge). In Polish tradition the first party after moving in was once called 'setting in'.
comments: etymology NOT verified; source only confirms housewarming customs; reviewer must check

text: On the morning itself, you can take up to four days off a year, and the boss can rarely say no.
note: Poland's 'urlop na żądanie' (leave on demand) comes out of the normal holiday allowance. You ask by the first day of leave; employers need an exceptional reason to refuse.
comments: courts allow refusal in rare cases, so 'rarely say no' is hedged

text: When a public holiday lands on a Saturday, employees get another weekday off in exchange.
note: Polish labour law counts a Saturday holiday as time already off, so the employer must grant a replacement day within the same settlement period. Freelance contracts don't get it.
comments: other countries may have similar compensation rules (fits guess)

text: Cheering before the result is in is discouraged: 'don't praise the day before sunset'.
note: Polish 'Nie chwal dnia przed zachodem słońca', Ukrainian 'Ne khvaly dnia do vechora': the local 'don't count your chickens before they hatch'.

text: On a sunny beach day, families hammer in colourful fabric windbreaks and fence off their patch of sand.
note: Polish 'parawaning' means building a wall of windbreaks to claim beach space (some resorts now limit it). Windscreens are also common on windy Dutch beaches.

text: Winter school holidays start on different weeks in different regions, so ski resorts fill up in turns.
note: Poland staggers 'ferie zimowe' by voivodeship, France uses zones A, B and C, and the Netherlands splits its February break into north, middle and south.

text: Joining a queue at a clinic or market stall, you ask who is last, then wander off, trusting everyone to keep your place.
fits: PL UA IT TR BR MX
note: Polish 'kto ostatni?', Ukrainian 'хто останній?', Italian 'chi è l'ultimo?': you note who you follow, then rely on the order.
comments: TR BR MX fits added on caution, unverified; source only loosely supports it

text: Ticket inspectors on trams and buses look like ordinary passengers until they pull out a badge.
note: Polish 'kanary' often work in plain clothes; plainclothes controllers also check tickets on French, Dutch and Italian transit.
comments: source is 2012 and mentions uniforms in some cities

text: Mums tell kids to dress 'like an onion', in thin layers to peel off as the day warms up.
note: Polish 'ubierać się na cebulkę'. A similar layering image exists in Ukrainian.

text: In mid-May, gardeners hold off planting tender seedlings until a short cold snap with its own nickname has passed.
note: Polish 'zimni ogrodnicy' and 'zimna Zośka' (12-15 May), French 'saints de glace', Dutch 'ijsheiligen'. Named after saints' days, but secular garden lore.
comments: saint-day names; flag for religion check

text: A cough is treated with a spoonful of chopped onion left to sit in sugar or honey until it turns into syrup.
note: Polish grandmothers swear by onion syrup ('syrop z cebuli'); Ukrainian families use similar onion and honey remedies.

text: A personal ID number that starts with your birth date is asked for at the doctor, the pharmacy and the post office.
note: Poland's PESEL has 11 digits and starts with the birth date. Korea's resident number, Italy's tax code and Mexico's CURP also encode it.
comments: fits for IT/MX: codes contain birth date but are not purely numeric; check

text: A slip in the mailbox says a registered letter is waiting at the post office, and if you ignore it a second slip follows.
note: Polish 'awizo': you get about two weeks to collect it with ID, then it goes back to the sender. Italy and France use a similar notice slip.
comments: second awizo comes from postal contracts; UA/BR fits unverified

text: When filing the yearly tax return, you can send 1% of your tax to a charity by writing in its registration number.
note: Poland's '1%' goes to a public-benefit organisation chosen by its KRS number. Italy's 'cinque per mille' works the same way with 0.5% of tax.

text: School marks run from 1 to 6, where 6 is the best and 1 is a fail, and teachers add plus and minus signs.
note: Polish marks run 1 (fail) to 6 (excellent), and the plus and minus signs are informal. In many other countries 1 is the top mark.

text: At the school entrance, kids change from outdoor shoes into indoor ones and leave their coats in the cloakroom.
note: Polish 'obuwie zmienne', Ukrainian 'zminne vzuttia' and Korean indoor slippers keep classroom floors clean, especially in winter.
comments: source only covers PL; UA/KR from general knowledge

text: Guests keep shouting "bitter!" during the party until the newlyweds kiss to sweeten the drinks.
note: Polish 'Gorzko, gorzko!' and Ukrainian 'Hirko!' ring out through the night; the kiss is the 'sugar'.

text: At midnight, the bride's veil is taken off and replaced with a cap or scarf, followed by party games.
note: This tradition marks the bride's move into married life. Today it is mostly games such as bouquet and tie tosses.

text: The wedding continues the next day with leftovers, soup and the same guests, as a party of its own.
note: Polish 'poprawiny' is the day-after party, often at the bride's family home. Some Ukrainian regions also celebrate a second day.

text: A proper lunch starts with a bowl of soup; a meal without one feels unfinished.
note: Polish 'zupa' and Ukrainian 'суп' open the midday meal, followed by a main course. A sweet fruit drink often comes along.

text: A slice of bread that falls on the floor gets picked up and kissed as a sign of respect.
note: Bread was precious in hard times. Polish and Ukrainian grandparents did this, and in Türkiye bread is kissed and touched to the forehead.
comments: folk custom with religious background, flag for review

text: In their first weeks at school, first-graders are 'knighted' with a giant pencil tapped on the shoulder.
note: Polish 'pasowanie na ucznia': the children pledge to study hard, then the head teacher 'knights' each one with a big pencil.

text: Wedding rings are worn on the right hand.
note: Right-hand wedding rings are traditional in Poland and Ukraine; Brazilian and Turkish couples wear engagement rings on the right, and some Dutch do too.
comments: check TR, BR and NL: engagement vs wedding ring

text: To a naive person who misses the obvious, people say: 'Did you fall off the Christmas tree?'
note: Polish 'z choinki się urwałeś?' roughly means 'were you born yesterday?'

text: A hopeless search is called 'looking for the wind in a field'.
note: Polish 'szukać wiatru w polu': looking for something already gone, so the effort is wasted.

text: Before a long trip, everyone sits down in silence for a moment "for the road".
note: A short quiet pause before leaving (prysisty na dorizhku) is meant to bring a safe journey.

text: People avoid shaking hands or passing things across a doorway.
note: Greeting across the threshold is said to bring a quarrel, so people step in or out first.

text: If you go back home for something you forgot, you look in a mirror before leaving again.
note: Turning back is said to bring bad luck; a glance in the mirror (some also stick out their tongue) 'cancels' it.

text: Whistling indoors is frowned upon, because it will "whistle away your money".
note: Older relatives will stop you mid-tune: 'Don't whistle, or there'll be no money!'

text: Summer weekends mean the family plot outside town, growing tomatoes and potatoes.
note: The 'dacha' or garden plot (PL 'działka') is a weekend retreat; many families grow a real share of their own vegetables.

text: Flowers for a host come in an odd number of stems; even numbers are for funerals.
note: Florists will add or remove a stem for you. Even bouquets are kept for mourning, so mind it on birthdays too.

text: Turning down food once is never accepted; the host keeps offering until you take more.
note: Feeding guests well is a point of pride. A first 'no' is read as modesty, so expect 'just a little more!'

text: Single guests are told not to sit at the corner of the table, or they won't marry for seven years.
note: A popular superstition in Ukraine and Poland: the corner seat means seven years without a wedding, so people shuffle to avoid it.

text: If you're given a knife as a gift, you hand back a coin so it counts as a purchase.
note: Sharp gifts are said to 'cut' a friendship; a symbolic coin turns the gift into a sale. Some do the same for watches.

text: Older relatives warn you never to sit on a cold stone or concrete step.
note: Cold surfaces get blamed for all kinds of illness; grandmas carry a cushion or a newspaper for park benches.

text: On the first day of school, kids dress up smartly and bring big bouquets for the teacher.
note: 1 September is the 'Day of Knowledge': a school-yard ceremony, smart outfits and flowers for every teacher.

text: At a wedding, parents greet the couple with a big round bread and salt.
note: The decorated wedding bread (UA 'korovai', PL 'korowaj') with salt stands for plenty; in some families, whoever takes the bigger bite will 'rule the house'.

text: Celebrating a birthday early is avoided, and early wishes are politely turned down.
note: Congratulating someone before the date is said to bring bad luck, so parties are held on the day or after it.

text: Asked "How are you?", the standard answer is simply "normal".
note: 'Normalno' means 'fine, nothing special'. Saying 'great!' can sound like boasting or tempting fate.

text: The older women on the bench by the building know everyone's business.
note: The grannies on the bench are a classic figure: informal neighbourhood watch, news agency and fashion critics.

text: After boasting about good luck, people knock on wood and spit three times over the left shoulder.
note: The spitting is pretend: you'll just hear 'tfu-tfu-tfu' said out loud, plus three knocks, to keep bad luck away.

text: "Yeah, right now!" said with a smirk actually means "not a chance".
note: 'Aha, zaraz!' is classic sarcasm. Compare Mexico's 'ahorita', where 'now' might mean later.

text: Shown a new purchase, people say "wear it in good health".
note: 'Nosy na zdorovya' (PL 'noś na zdrowie') is the standard reply to new clothes, shoes or even a new phone.

text: Threatening to "show you where the crayfish spend winter" means you're about to be taught a lesson.
note: The idiom ('pokazaty, de raky zymuiut') exists in Polish too; crayfish hide deep in the mud in winter, a cold place to be.

text: Food gets cute names: a "little cucumber", a "little piece of bread", a "little cup of tea".
note: Diminutives make an offer warmer: Ukrainian 'ohirochok', Polish 'chlebek', Mexican 'cafecito', Brazilian 'cafezinho', Dutch 'koffietje'.

text: A manager or teacher is addressed by first name plus their father's name.
note: The patronymic shows respect for bosses, teachers and elders; younger workplaces are moving to first names.

text: Accountants, teachers and IT workers each have an official day in the calendar, with cards and cake at work.
note: Dozens of professions have a 'professional day'; colleagues and clients send greetings, a habit from the 20th century.

text: A comic curse for someone annoying: "may a duck kick you!"
note: 'Shchob tebe kachka kopnula!' belongs to a family of cartoonish curses, like 'may a cat sneeze on you'.

text: When a child says thank you, adults reply "grow big!"
note: 'Rosty velykyi!' (or 'velyka' for a girl) replaces 'you're welcome', mostly with kids and sometimes jokingly with adults.

text: Say "thank you" for a meal and you're told "to your health".
note: 'Na zdorovia' is a warm 'you're welcome', especially after food; Poles answer thanks for a meal the same way.

text: To wrap up a rambling story, people just say "shorter…" and carry on.
note: 'Korotshe' works like 'anyway' or 'long story short', even when the story then gets longer.

text: Playing a dirty trick on someone is "planting a pig" on them.
note: 'Pidsunuty svyniu' (PL 'podłożyć świnię').

text: Waiting for something that won't come is "waiting for weather from the sea".
note: 'Chekaty z moria pohody'.

text: "A word is not a sparrow": once it's out, you can't catch it.
note: 'Slovo ne horobets, vyletyt – ne spiimaiesh': think before you speak.

text: Two people with the same bad habits are "two boots, a pair".
note: 'Dva choboty – para': two of a kind, usually said with a sigh.

text: One small flaw that spoils something good is "a spoon of tar in a barrel of honey".
note: 'Lozhka dohtiu v bochtsi medu'; Poles say the same.

text: After a brutal week at work, you feel like a "squeezed lemon".
note: 'Vychavlenyi lymon': completely drained. The French and Poles squeeze the same lemon.

text: On one Thursday in May, colleagues and students come in wearing embroidered shirts.
note: Vyshyvanka Day (third Thursday of May) was started in 2006 by a student in Chernivtsi; it's a celebration, not an official holiday.

text: At the end of school, a graduate carries a first-grader on their shoulder, ringing a hand bell.
note: The 'last bell' ceremony in late May also has sashes, a school waltz and lots of tears.

text: Parents post baby photos with a sticker over the face, so nobody can jinx the baby.
note: A belief that a child can be cursed through a photo; Turkish parents worry about the evil eye in the same way.

text: A safety pin hidden on clothing protects against the evil eye.
note: Mostly pinned on children; a pin that darkens is said to show someone wished you harm.

text: You never give an empty wallet as a gift; there's always at least a coin inside.
note: An empty wallet means an empty year, so the giver adds a coin or a note for luck.

text: On midsummer night, couples jump over a bonfire holding hands, and girls float flower wreaths.
note: Ivana Kupala: if the hands stay joined, the couple will marry. Poles celebrate 'Noc Kupały' too.

text: Children call any adult stranger "uncle" or "auntie".
note: 'Diadko' and 'titka' are polite for kids; Turkish children say 'amca' and 'teyze', Korean ones 'ajeossi' and 'ajumma'.

text: On a shared minibus, you pass your fare hand to hand through the passengers to the driver, and the change comes back the same way.
note: Ukrainian marshrutka, Turkish dolmuş and Mexican combi all run on stranger-to-stranger trust: fares and change are relayed along the seats.
comments: MX fits guess; some UA cities pay on exit

text: Older women sell herbs, pickles and flowers from a crate or a rug near the metro exit.
note: Informal stalls near stations top up small pensions, and the produce is often homegrown.

text: Visiting a home with children, you bring a cake for the table and something sweet for the kids.
note: A cake is a classic thank-you for the host, and children in the house may expect a sweet. Meals usually end with cake and tea or coffee.
comments: PL and TR fits are guesses; fairly generic

text: Wishing luck before an exam, you say 'neither fluff nor feather', and the answer is 'go to hell'.
note: 'Ni pukha, ni pera!' – 'Do bisa!' Hunters feared forest spirits would spoil a hunt if they heard a wish for success, so they wished the opposite. Still said before exams.
comments: similar phrases may exist in neighbouring languages (fits guess); same habit type as it-026

text: Kids are sent to spend the summer holidays in their grandparents' village, running free until September.
note: A summer with grandparents in the countryside is a classic childhood memory for many Ukrainian, Polish and Turkish families.
comments: source is a 1998 article about grandparents minding kids; low confidence on PL and TR

text: On the first long weekend of May, friends drive out of town to grill marinated meat skewers by a river or in a forest.
note: Ukrainian 'mayivka' and Polish 'majówka': the May holidays open the outdoor grilling season.
comments: Polish majówka grilling not separately sourced

text: A newborn gets a birth certificate, a tax number and baby benefits from one online application, with no queue at any office.
note: Ukraine's 'eMalyatko' in the Diia app bundles the birth registration and several benefits into a single request.
comments: overlaps thematically with ua-007 (Diia); different habit

text: School marks run from 1 to 12, where 12 is the best and the lowest three points mean the topic is not mastered.
note: Ukraine's 12-point scale is used for semester and yearly marks. Schools may use their own scale but must convert it.

text: Each class's parent group collects cash for curtains, repairs and teacher gifts, and saying no feels awkward.
note: Ukrainian schools officially ban compulsory collections, yet class funds persist. Polish 'rada rodziców' and Mexican parent fees are similar.

text: Before the ceremony, the groom and his friends must "buy" the bride through jokes, riddles and a bit of cash.
note: Ukrainian 'vykup nevisty' is a staged ransom at the door. Polish wedding gates ('bramy') and Turkish door games are similar.

text: A professional host runs the wedding party with toasts, contests and dance games.
note: The Ukrainian 'tamada' or 'vedučyj' and the Polish 'wodzirej' keep the party moving between dances.

text: The couple stand on an embroidered towel, and whoever steps on it first is said to rule the household.
note: Ukrainian 'рушник' custom; Turkish couples race to step on each other's foot first for the same idea.

text: When an outcome is uncertain, people say 'grandma told fortunes both ways'.
note: Ukrainian 'надвоє баба ворожила': it could go either way, so don't count on it yet.

text: Something that happens out of the blue 'neither sat nor fell'.
note: Ukrainian 'ні сіло, ні впало' describes a random remark or a sudden event with no reason.

text: At a birthday party, you congratulate the parents, partner and friends of the birthday person too.
note: The Dutch say 'gefeliciteerd!' to everyone close to the birthday person, not just to them.

text: A friend visiting in the late afternoon says "I'll leave now, so you can have dinner".
note: Dinner is early and usually planned; staying over dinner time without an invitation is unusual.

text: Cycling through heavy rain is just part of the commute.
note: With more bikes than people, weather is no excuse; rain trousers and ponchos are standard kit.

text: Curtains often stay open in the evening, so you can see right into people's living rooms.
note: Open curtains are an old habit, sometimes explained as 'we have nothing to hide'; staring in is still impolite.

text: Coffee with a friend gets booked in the calendar two weeks ahead.
note: The 'agenda' rules social life; dropping by unannounced is rare, even among close friends and family.

text: Furniture goes into the flat through a window, lifted up from the street, because the stairs are too steep.
note: Old houses have a hoisting beam at the top for this; today movers bring a platform lift up to the window.

text: At a birthday party, guests sit in a big circle of chairs in the living room.
note: At a 'kringverjaardag' (circle birthday) you walk around the circle on arrival, shaking hands and congratulating everyone.

text: Guests usually keep their shoes on inside the house.
note: Shoes on is the norm in most homes, though more families now ask guests to take them off.

text: A party invitation states an end time, and guests actually leave around then.
note: Clear plans count as polite: a children's party 'from 2 to 5' means parents are at the door at 5.

text: Birthdays are written on a calendar that hangs in the toilet.
note: The 'verjaardagskalender' has no year or weekdays, so it lasts forever, and the loo is where you see it every day.

text: On one spring holiday, people sell their old stuff on blankets in the street.
note: On King's Day (27 April), the 'vrijmarkt' (free market) lets anyone sell without a permit; kids sell toys and play music for coins.

text: In the weeks before 5 December, kids leave a shoe by the fireplace and find sweets in it the next morning.
note: Sinterklaas season starts mid-November: children sing songs and leave a carrot for his horse. Polish kids find treats in their shoes on 6 December.

text: When a baby is born, visitors are served rusks topped with pink or blue sugared seeds.
note: 'Beschuit met muisjes' (rusk with 'little mice'): the aniseed sprinkles look like tiny mice. Pink for a girl, blue for a boy.

text: For a week after a birth, a nurse visits the new family at home every day.
note: 'Kraamzorg' is covered by insurance: the nurse checks mother and baby, teaches bathing, and even helps around the house.

text: Gifts come with a rhyming poem that gently roasts the person who receives them.
note: Around 5 December, 'surprises' come with a Sinterklaas poem; everyone reads theirs aloud, and the teasing is half the fun.

text: Before cycling anywhere, people check a rain radar app to dodge the next shower.
note: Buienradar (rain radar) is one of the most-used apps; timing a ride between showers is a real skill and a small-talk topic.

text: Compliment someone's new jacket and they'll proudly tell you how cheap it was.
note: Thrift is a point of pride, so a compliment is often answered with the price and where the deal was found.

text: Cycling against the wind is the go-to excuse for being late, and a badge of honour.
note: 'Tegenwind' (headwind) is a real struggle on flat land; there's even a headwind cycling championship held during storms.

text: "Act normal, that's crazy enough" is common advice.
note: 'Doe normaal, dan doe je al gek genoeg' sums up the dislike of showing off or standing out.

text: One all-purpose word means tasty, cosy, comfy and nice: for food, weather, sleep or a job well done.
note: 'Lekker' covers it all: lekker eten, lekker weer, lekker slapen. 'Lekker bezig!' means 'nice going!'

text: "Not bad" or "not wrong" is a sincere compliment.
note: 'Niet verkeerd' (not wrong) or 'niet slecht' (not bad) can mean 'actually really good'; big praise is used sparingly.

text: There's one word for cosy, sociable and fun at once, used for homes, cafés and evenings.
note: 'Gezellig' has no exact English match; a place or evening that's 'ongezellig' feels cold and unsociable.

text: "Now the monkey comes out of the sleeve" means the real reason is finally revealed.
note: 'Nu komt de aap uit de mouw' comes from street performers who hid a monkey in their sleeve for the trick's finale.

text: Telling your boss "this plan won't work" in a meeting counts as helpful.
note: Directness is valued over diplomacy; blunt feedback is rarely meant as rude, and juniors are expected to speak up.

text: Lunch at work is often bread with cheese and a glass of milk, eaten in half an hour.
note: Hot food is for dinner; office canteens serve sandwiches and milk, and many people bring bread from home.

text: On your birthday, you bring cake or treats for your colleagues.
note: The birthday person brings the snacks: the Dutch call it 'trakteren', and Polish, Ukrainian and Italian offices know the habit too.

text: Working four days a week is very common, especially for mothers.
note: About half of all workers are part-time (around 70% of women and 28% of men); a weekday off with the kids is a 'mamadag' or 'papadag'.

text: Meetings aim for everyone to agree, so decisions take long but rarely get reversed.
note: The 'poldermodel', consensus through long talks, is said to come from working together to keep the water out.

text: On someone's 50th birthday, a big doll of an old man or woman appears in their front garden.
note: Turning 50 means you 'see Abraham' (men) or 'see Sarah' (women); posters, dolls and even inflatables tell the whole street.

text: Once a month at midday, warning sirens wail across the country, and nobody even looks up.
note: The national warning sirens are tested on the first Monday of the month at noon; staying calm is a sign you've 'gone Dutch'.

text: Parents carry two or three toddlers in a wooden box on the front of their bike.
note: The 'bakfiets' (box bike) is a family car on two wheels; it also moves groceries, Christmas trees and furniture.

text: Friends greet each other with three kisses on the cheeks.
note: Right, left, right. Expats lose count, and many younger people now settle for one or a hug.

text: A slap on the knees and a two-note sigh mean the visit is over.
note: 'Hè hè!' plus a knee slap is the classic signal that it's time to go home (or to start dinner).

text: At 15 degrees and cloudy, someone fires up the barbecue and calls it summer.
note: Any dry spell is seized on; 'BBQ weather' starts much earlier than visitors expect.

text: The lock on a bike is often worth more than the bike itself.
note: People ride cheap old bikes with heavy locks because bike theft is so common, and the bike still gets stolen.

text: Delicious food is "like an angel peeing on your tongue".
note: 'Alsof er een engeltje over je tong piest' is high praise for the cook, however odd it sounds.

text: Try the local language in a shop and the cashier answers in fluent English.
note: A famous hurdle for learners; finally getting a reply in Dutch is celebrated like a diploma.

text: There's a special word for walking on a windy beach to clear your head.
note: 'Uitwaaien' (to blow out): a brisk walk in the wind to refresh body and mind.

text: There's one word for the fun of looking forward to a party or a trip.
note: 'Voorpret' (pre-fun): enjoying the planning and anticipation, sometimes more than the event itself.

text: Getting a taste of your own medicine is getting "a cookie of your own dough".
note: 'Een koekje van eigen deeg krijgen': being treated the way you treated others.

text: Something bought dirt cheap was bought "for an apple and an egg".
note: 'Voor een appel en een ei' fits nicely with the national love of a bargain.

text: "Unfortunately, peanut butter!" is a jokey way to say "tough luck".
note: 'Helaas, pindakaas' works because it rhymes; kids and adults both use it.

text: Small talk is "talking about little cows and calves".
note: 'Over koetjes en kalfjes praten': chatting about nothing in particular.

text: Every May, an extra 8% of last year's salary lands in your account for the holidays.
note: 'Vakantiegeld' (holiday allowance) is a legal minimum, usually paid in May or June.

text: On Friday afternoon, the office empties into the canteen for snacks and drinks with colleagues.
note: The 'vrijmibo' (short for Friday-afternoon get-together), with bitterballen and chat, weekly or monthly.

text: Public transport needs a tap on the way out as well, or you are charged a high default fare.
note: Dutch OV-chipkaart: forget to check out and you pay the full boarding fare, refundable online. Korea's T-money also needs an exit tap for transfers.

text: Car drivers and passengers open the door with the hand farthest from it, so they turn their head and see passing cyclists.
note: The 'Dutch reach' makes your body twist towards the mirror; it spread abroad as a way to prevent car-door crashes with cyclists.
comments: unclear if taught officially in driving tests

text: Two friends share one bike, with the passenger sitting sideways on the rear rack, and no one thinks it odd.
note: Dutch city bikes come with a rear rack that carries groceries, kids and friends; riding double is an everyday way to get home.
comments: source is a tongue-in-cheek student paper

text: One evening a week the shops stay open late, and on other evenings they close around six.
note: 'Koopavond' (shopping evening) is traditionally Thursday in cities and Friday in towns; it is fading as Sunday opening grows.
comments: fading, 2014 source plus NL Times update

text: If you are out, the courier rings a neighbour, and you later collect your parcel from their door.
note: Couriers try a neighbour first and tell you by message where the parcel ended up. It is why a short 'do you have my parcel?' knock is normal.
comments: FR fit is a guess (gardien/neighbours often take parcels)

text: From intern to CEO, everyone is on a first-name basis.
note: Dutch workplaces are flat and managers go by first name. American offices are informal too, but open disagreement with the boss is especially expected in the Netherlands.
comments: traditional Dutch firms may differ; US fit is a guess

text: Each December, employers hand staff a Christmas hamper or a gift voucher.
note: Dutch 'kerstpakket' (about 7.4 million employees get a pack or card); Italian 'cesto natalizio', often with panettone. Many firms now let staff pick a gift.
comments: Italian side backed only by commercial/blog sources (fits guess)

text: Standing out is discouraged with a saying: the head above the field gets chopped off.
note: 'Als je je kop boven het maaiveld uitsteekt, wordt hij eraf gehakt.' A TU Delft piece says it's often used to shrug off criticism, though it holds 'a grain of truth'.
comments: close in spirit to nl-021; Australian 'tall poppy' is similar but outside the ten

text: On New Year's Eve, families watch a comedian run through the year's news in one long monologue.
note: The 'oudejaarsconference' began with Wim Kan's radio show in 1954 and is now a TV tradition, often watched with fried dough balls.
comments: the genre is political satire, text avoids it; flag against the politics rule; 1954 date from a search summary

text: People answer the phone by saying their own name, with the word 'with' in front.
note: 'Met Pim': a bare 'hello' can sound abrupt. Skip your name and the caller may ask 'met wie spreek ik?' (with whom am I speaking?).
comments: 'rude' claim comes from one commenter, softened in the note

text: On 1 January, thousands in matching orange woolly hats run into the cold sea together, then warm up with hot soup.
note: The Dutch 'nieuwjaarsduik' draws crowds at dozens of beaches; New Year plunges also happen in Poland and the US.
comments: PL/US fits are from general knowledge

text: Parents sign young kids up for lessons that end with swimming diplomas in levels A, B and C.
note: The Dutch Zwem-ABC diploma system, strengthened after the 1953 floods, is a normal part of childhood; many families see the certificates as essential.

text: Even in stations and many cafés you drop coins into a turnstile or an attendant's saucer to use the toilet.
note: Paid public toilets (around 50 cents) are standard in the Netherlands and also common in Poland, Ukraine, Türkiye and Italy.
comments: fits PL UA TR IT from general knowledge

text: On the first sunny spring day, café terraces fill instantly and chairs get turned to face the sun, coat on or not.
note: Dutch terraces fill at the first ray of sun; French and Italian cafés behave the same.

text: The weather forecast counts 'summer days' above 25 degrees and 'tropical days' above 30 as official categories.
note: The Dutch weather service (KNMI) counts 'zomerse dagen' (25+) and 'tropische dagen' (30+), and news and chat repeat the count.
comments: AI-generated; terms are right, not sure how much the public uses them

text: To renew a passport or register a move, you book a time slot online first, and turning up without one gets you sent away.
note: Dutch town halls work 'op afspraak' (by appointment) for passports and registration; walk-in hours are rare. Others do this for popular services.
comments: source is general gov page; check appointment-only claim

text: Every autumn, people compare their compulsory health insurance and often switch insurer before the 31 December deadline.
note: Dutch insurers can be changed every January, and the new insurer cancels the old policy for you. US employers run a similar 'open enrollment' each autumn.

text: Children start school on the very day they turn four, joining a class in the middle of the school year.
note: Dutch kids start 'groep 1' on their fourth birthday, after a few trial days; school becomes compulsory at five.

text: At about age 12, a teacher's advice decides which type of secondary school a child goes to: practical, middle or university track.
note: Dutch 'schooladvies' from group 8 sets the track: vmbo, havo or vwo. Switching later is possible, but the first advice weighs heavily.

text: Guests are split into groups: some are invited for the whole day, some just to the afternoon drinks, some just to the evening party.
note: Dutch 'daggasten', 'receptiegasten' and 'avondgasten' are on separate lists, partly because couples pay for the wedding themselves.

text: A friend is put in charge of running the wedding day: the schedule, the speeches and the surprises.
note: The Dutch 'ceremoniemeester' is not the legal witness. The US best man or maid of honour covers part of this job.

text: Cheese for bread is shaved into thin, even slices with a flat slicer, not cut into chunks.
note: The Dutch 'kaasschaaf' sits in nearly every kitchen drawer; thin slices make a few grams of cheese cover a whole sandwich.
comments: Wikipedia only; Dutch-specific claim not sourced

text: Dinner often ends with a bowl of smooth, pourable custard or yoghurt rather than cake.
note: Dutch 'vla' comes in cartons from the supermarket; vanilla and chocolate are the classics, eaten with a spoon after the hot meal.

text: When a teenager passes the final school exams, a school bag is hung from the flagpole outside the house.
note: Dutch 'tas aan de vlag': the bag shows the results are in and passed. Whole streets fly bags in the same week of June.

text: A wooden stork, a sign with the baby's name and balloons appear in the front garden when a baby is born.
note: Dutch 'ooievaar' and 'geboortebord' decorations stay up for weeks, long after the first visitors have come and gone.

text: Couples throw a small party at 12.5 years of marriage, halfway to the silver anniversary.
note: Dutch 'koperen bruiloft' (copper wedding): the half-way party is popular enough that shops sell cards and gifts for it.
comments: retailer source; also marked in Denmark and Germany

text: Very heavy rain is described as 'raining pipe stems'.
note: Dutch 'het regent pijpenstelen': long, thin clay pipe stems look like falling rain.

text: Handing someone anything, from change to a plate, you say the word for 'please'.
note: Dutch 'alsjeblieft' doubles as 'here you go'; Turkish 'buyurun' and Italian 'prego' do the same job.
comments: TR and IT fits from knowledge

text: A very easy task is called 'a little apple, a little egg'.
note: Dutch 'appeltje eitje' is the equivalent of 'piece of cake'; Van Dale added it just in 2005.
comments: source checked via search summary only

text: Arriving 30 minutes late to a house party is normal; arriving on time can feel awkward.
note: Party start times are loose, and hosts are often still getting ready at the stated time.

text: Friends greet with one, two or three cheek kisses, depending on which city they're from.
note: In Brazil the number of kisses varies by region: often one in São Paulo, two in Rio.

text: Used toilet paper goes in a small bin next to the toilet, not down the drain.
note: Many older pipes and septic tanks can't handle paper, so a small lidded bin sits next to the toilet.

text: Shops show prices as "10 interest-free payments of 30", even for shoes or a fan.
note: Paying in instalments on a credit card is standard ('parcelado' in Brazil, 'taksit' in Türkiye); the number of instalments can matter more than the total.

text: Instant payments by phone number or QR code are used for everything, even at street stalls.
note: Pix, launched by the central bank in 2020, became the default way to pay within months; vendors display a QR code.

text: At checkout, the cashier asks if you want your tax ID number on the receipt.
note: 'CPF na nota?' Adding your CPF number to receipts can earn small tax refunds and prize-draw entries in some states.

text: Apartment buildings have a doorman who takes in parcels and knows everyone's routine.
note: Brazil's 'porteiro', Türkiye's 'kapıcı' and the security guard of a Korean apartment block: gatekeeper, parcel desk and local news source in one.

text: Saying goodbye takes an hour: you announce you're leaving, then keep chatting at the door.
note: Leaving without a hug or a word for each person is rude, and new topics always come up on the way out.

text: "Come by my place sometime!" is a warm thing to say, not a real invitation.
note: 'Aparece lá em casa!' signals friendliness; wait for a day and an address before showing up.

text: Visitors at a house with a gate clap their hands to call the owner instead of knocking.
note: 'Bater palmas' (clapping) works when the door is far behind a wall or gate; doorbells were long a luxury.

text: Every visitor, even a repair person, is offered a tiny cup of sweet coffee.
note: The 'cafezinho' is a gesture of welcome; turning it down is fine, but offering it is almost automatic.

text: Kids' birthday parties are big events at a party hall, with a decorated sweets table.
note: Kids' parties at a party hall ('buffet infantil' in Brazil, 'salón de fiestas' in Mexico) can rival weddings; the decorated sweets table is the photo spot.

text: After the birthday song, everyone asks who will get the first slice of cake.
note: Who gets 'o primeiro pedaço' (the first slice) is a public choice, often a parent or partner, and a chance for teasing.

text: On New Year's Eve, people dress in white and jump over seven waves at the beach.
note: Each wave comes with a wish; many also pick a colour of clothing for luck: yellow for money, pink for love.

text: In June, schools and towns throw country-style festivals with square dancing and costumes.
note: 'Festas Juninas' celebrate the June saints' days and country life; kids dress up as country folk and dance the 'quadrilha'.

text: Couples celebrate Valentine's Day in June, not February.
note: 'Dia dos Namorados' (12 June) was set in 1949 by an advertising man to boost sales in a slow month; February is often Carnival.

text: Laughing in a text message is typed as "kkkkk".
note: Brazilians type 'kkkk' because 'k' sounds like 'ca' in Portuguese; Koreans type 'ㅋㅋㅋ' (kekeke), the same idea in their own alphabet.

text: "Let's set a date!" is how friends say goodbye, and the date never gets set.
note: Brazil's 'vamos marcar!', Korea's 'let's have a meal sometime' and the American 'let's grab coffee' are warm goodbyes, not real plans.

text: Relatives post "good morning" pictures with flowers and glitter in the family group chat every day.
note: Family WhatsApp groups are an institution; the daily 'bom dia' image (MX 'buenos días') is a running joke.

text: People joke that the year doesn't really start until Carnival is over.
note: Carnival falls in February or March, and big projects and decisions are half-seriously put off until it's over.

text: A thumbs-up is the all-purpose "OK, thanks, got it".
note: The 'joinha' is used to thank a driver, agree, or say hi. The 'OK' circle hand sign, though, is rude.

text: There's a word for finding a clever way around a rule or problem.
note: Brazilians call it 'jeitinho', Italians 'arrangiarsi': admirable resourcefulness or bending the rules, depending on who you ask.

text: "All good?" "All beauty!" is a normal greeting.
note: 'Tudo bem?' 'Tudo bom!' or just 'Beleza?' (beauty?) open countless conversations.

text: Chipping in money as a group is called "making a little cow".
note: BR 'fazer uma vaquinha', MX 'hacer una vaca'. In Brazil it's linked to an old numbers game where the cow is number 25.

text: "Paying the monkey" means embarrassing yourself in public.
note: 'Pagar mico' comes from an old card game where whoever was left holding the monkey card lost.

text: Many people, even famous ones, are known by a single nickname.
note: From footballers to TV hosts, nicknames ('apelidos') often replace full names, and '-inho' endings make them friendlier.

text: Office workers brush their teeth in the office bathroom after lunch.
note: Brushing after every meal is a strong habit in Brazil and Korea, so desks hide toothbrush kits and office sinks get busy around 1 pm.

text: By law, workers get a 13th month's salary, paid around Christmas.
note: Brazil's 'décimo terceiro' and Italy's 'tredicesima' are a full extra month's pay before Christmas, and they fuel holiday shopping.

text: Work emails end with "a hug", even to people you've never met.
note: 'Abraço' or just 'Abs' is a standard sign-off; stiff formality can read as cold.

text: Lunch near the office is a buffet where you pay by the weight of your plate.
note: 'Comida a quilo' restaurants are the default quick lunch: you serve yourself, then the plate goes on a scale.

text: Every Christmas, an uncle asks if the layered dessert is "for looking or for eating".
note: 'É pavê ou pá comê?': 'pavê' sounds like 'pra ver' (to look at). The teller is lovingly called 'tio do pavê'.

text: After the birthday song, guests sing a teasing verse asking who the birthday person will marry.
note: 'Com quem será?' (who will it be?) is call-and-response, and the crowd shouts out a name.

text: Pretending not to see someone you'd rather avoid is called "doing the Egyptian".
note: 'Fazer a egípcia': you turn your face away, like the side-on figures in Egyptian paintings.

text: An improvised fix held together with tape is a national art form with its own word.
note: 'Gambiarra' is said with pride and self-mockery, from wiring hacks to code workarounds.

text: A stingy person is said to have "a cow's hand".
note: 'Mão de vaca'; 'pão-duro' (hard bread) means the same.

text: Being the third wheel on a date is "holding the candle".
note: 'Segurar vela'. Italians 'reggono il moccolo' and the French 'tiennent la chandelle': same candle, same awkwardness.

text: Standing someone up is "giving them a cake".
note: 'Dar um bolo': no cake is actually involved.

text: Letting a friend down or saying the wrong thing is "stepping on the ball".
note: 'Pisar na bola' comes, of course, from football.

text: Doing someone a small favour is "breaking a branch" for them.
note: 'Quebrar um galho' means helping out or making do with what you have.

text: On Fridays, office chats fill up with one word: Friday turned into a verb.
note: 'Sextou!' (roughly 'it Fridayed!') from 'sexta' (Friday), made popular by a 2015 song.

text: Padding a report or a meeting with filler is "stuffing sausage".
note: 'Encher linguiça' comes from filling sausage casings with scraps when the good meat ran out.

text: Bosses, teachers and doctors are called by first name, with "Mr" or "Mrs" in front.
note: 'Seu João', 'Dona Maria': warm and respectful at once. Using a surname can sound cold.

text: After the birthday song, everyone breaks into a fast chant and cheers like a marching band.
note: 'É pique, é pique… é hora, é hora… rá-tim-bum!' follows 'Parabéns pra você'.

text: At a party before the baby is born, every guest brings packs of nappies in a size printed on the invitation.
note: At a 'chá de fraldas' (nappy tea), sizes are spread out so the baby won't outgrow them all at once.

text: In Secret Santa, each giver describes their person with teasing clues while everyone shouts guesses.
note: At 'amigo secreto', the person guessed walks up to cheers, then describes the next one; the reveal is the main event.

text: Children get presents on a special day in October, almost like a second Christmas.
note: Children's Day ('Dia das Crianças') is 12 October and a big date for toy shops.

text: Hot water comes from an electric heater built into the shower head.
note: The 'chuveiro elétrico' has a summer/winter switch; tens of millions of homes use one.

text: Signing a contract often means a trip to a notary to confirm the signature is really yours.
note: 'Reconhecer firma' at a 'cartório' is a routine errand; digital notary services are slowly cutting the queues.

text: Pizza and even chicken wings are eaten with a knife and fork.
note: Eating with your hands is rare at restaurants and parties; a napkin around the slice is the compromise.

text: Avocado is a sweet fruit, blended with milk and sugar into a smoothie.
note: 'Vitamina de abacate' is the classic; savoury avocado toast is the odd one out.

text: The restaurant bill arrives with an extra 10% already added for the waiter, and you can ask for it to be removed.
note: Brazil's 'taxa de serviço' is about 10% and optional; some Italian bills show 'servizio' and some Korean bills a service charge too.
comments: draft v3; fits guess for IT KR

text: Even in ordinary shops, people ask "any discount if I pay in cash?" and often get one.
note: Brazilian 'desconto à vista'; since a 2017 law, shops may price cash and card differently if they display it. Asking is routine in many countries.

text: At a red light or on the bus, a seller steps up to offer water, sweets or phone chargers, and passengers buy without fuss.
note: Vendors on buses, at traffic lights and in the metro are everyday sights in Brazil and Mexico, with vagoneros in the Mexico City metro.
comments: draft v3; metro-vendor part verified for MX, BR via Manaus study

text: On one morning a week, your street closes to cars and turns into a market of fruit, fish and fried snacks.
note: Brazil's 'feira livre' and Mexico's 'tianguis' rotate through neighbourhoods by weekday; fried pastel with sugarcane juice is a Brazilian feira classic.

text: People buy rice, oil and cleaning products by the case at a warehouse store open to everyone, not just shops.
note: Brazil's 'atacarejo' mixes wholesale and retail; US warehouse clubs work similarly but need a membership.

text: Residents book the building's party hall for birthdays, and whoever asks first gets the date.
note: 'Salão de festas' in Brazil, 'salón de eventos' in Mexico, 'clubhouse' in the US. House rules decide who may book, and holidays are often kept for the whole building.
comments: draft v3; MX and US fits are guesses

text: Before the wedding, the bride's friends throw an afternoon party where everyone brings a pot, a plate or a kitchen tool.
note: 'Chá de panela' (pot tea) in Brazil: each guest brings one kitchen item, often from the couple's list. The US bridal shower works much the same way.
comments: draft v3; US fit is a guess; MX may have a similar custom

text: At a friends' barbecue, each guest brings about a kilo of meat or chips in for the shopping.
note: Group barbecues are cheap because costs are shared: about 300 g of meat per person is the rule of thumb.
comments: draft v3; fits guess: AR/UY not in the ten; US potluck is close

text: By law, the weeks you take off come with an extra payment on top of your usual salary.
note: Brazil's 'terço de férias' adds a third of a month's pay; Mexico's 'prima vacacional' is at least 25% of holiday pay. The Dutch 'vakantiegeld' (8%) is similar.
comments: draft v3; NL fit is a guess (allowance not tied to taking leave); Mexican 25% figure from expansion.mx search result

text: At year's end, colleagues pool money for one shared lottery ticket, and each person gets a receipt for their share.
note: Brazil's 'bolão' (often for the 'Mega da Virada' draw) and the American 'office pool' work the same way: friends, family or coworkers buy shares of one bet.
comments: draft v3; source covers the rules, not how common it is at work; US fit is a guess

text: There's a word for non-stop joking and teasing among friends, and it names a style of internet memes too.
note: 'Zoeira': to tease ('zoar', 'tirar sarro') is affectionate, and being teased means you belong. Football banter and WhatsApp groups are prime territory.
comments: draft v3; meme sense from an academic paper seen in search, not opened; teasing culture also exists elsewhere (fits guess)

text: A reply to a question is often a voice note of several minutes, not a text.
note: Brazil's 'áudio' (WhatsApp's president says Brazilians send about four times more voice messages than any other country), Italian 'vocale', Turkish 'sesli mesaj'.
comments: draft v3; MX, IT and TR fits rest on language-blog claims

text: Asking for someone's number, people use a short nickname for the main chat app instead of its name.
note: 'Me passa seu zap?' ('zap' or 'zap-zap' is Brazilian shorthand for WhatsApp). Zuckerberg praised Brazilians for making 'Zap Zap' their own.
comments: draft v3; nickname confirmed in news text, the exact 'give me your zap' phrasing is my example

text: Replying with a sticker, often homemade from a friend's face, is routine.
note: Brazil's 'figurinhas' are often homemade; Korea's chat 'emoticons' are mostly bought character packs. Zuckerberg says Brazilians send more stickers than anyone.
comments: draft v3; KR half rests on an Asia Times article (asiatimes.com/?p=323265); 'homemade' detail from search results only

text: On the beach, vendors walk the sand shouting their wares, from grilled cheese on a stick to shrimp, right to your towel.
note: In Brazil, sellers grill 'queijo coalho' on portable stoves along the sand. Beach sellers also roam Mexican resorts.

text: On the beach, friends keep a ball in the air with feet and head, or rally a wooden paddle ball with no score.
note: Altinha, futevôlei and frescobol are beach games that grew up on Rio's sand in the 1940s to 1960s.

text: On Sundays, a big avenue closes to cars so people can walk, skate and cycle down the middle of it.
note: São Paulo's Avenida Paulista and Mexico City's Paseo de la Reforma (Muévete en Bici) both open to people on Sundays.

text: On a packed bus, a seated stranger will offer to hold your bag on their lap while you stand.
note: In a Brazilian study of bus trips, seated riders offered to hold standing riders' bags in about 60% of situations. The habit exists elsewhere too.
comments: draft v3; study is from 2001; other fits from general knowledge

text: A thumbs-up is the everyday way to say 'fine', while making a ring with thumb and forefinger counts as rude.

text: Couples celebrate every month of being together with a message or a small gift.

text: Giving up and no longer caring about consequences is 'kicking the bucket'.

text: "Right now" can mean in a minute, in an hour, or maybe never.
note: 'Ahorita', the diminutive of 'ahora' (now), is famously flexible; context tells you which one.

text: Everyone chants until the birthday person takes a bite of the cake, then someone pushes their face into it.
note: '¡Mordida!' The first bite and the gentle push into the cake is a classic Mexican birthday prank.

text: A truck crawls through the streets playing a recorded voice offering to buy old mattresses and fridges.
note: 'Se compran colchones, tambores, refrigeradores...' is so famous it became a meme, a song and a ringtone.

text: At the supermarket, an older person bags your groceries and works for tips.
note: Many stores have senior packers who rely on tips; the job used to go to teenagers nicknamed 'cerillos' (matches).

text: A man waves you into a parking spot with whistles, and expects a coin when you leave.
note: The 'viene viene' (come, come) guides drivers in and out; Brazil's 'flanelinha' does the same, whether you asked or not.

text: At the petrol station, an attendant fills the tank for you and gets a small tip.
note: Self-service is rare: the 'despachador' in Mexico, 'frentista' in Brazil and 'pompacı' in Türkiye fill up and may clean your windscreen too.

text: Hosts welcome you by saying their house is now your house.
note: 'Mi casa es tu casa' is meant warmly; you may also hear 'estás en tu casa' (you're in your home).

text: Giving their own address, people say "your house is at" before the street name.
note: Calling your own home 'su casa' ('your house, on Juárez Street') is a classic courtesy that confuses visitors.

text: Bringing a friend or two to a party without asking is fine: the more, the merrier.
note: Party guest lists are elastic, and hosts usually cook for more people than they invited.

text: There's a special word for staying at the table to chat long after the meal.
note: 'La sobremesa' can last longer than the meal itself, especially at Sunday lunch. The Dutch have a word for it too: 'natafelen'.

text: For a big family party, the street outside gets a rented tent, tables and chairs.
note: Renting a 'lona' (canopy) with folding tables is a cheap way to host 100 guests; neighbours usually join or tolerate the music.

text: Family members sing a morning serenade to wake up the birthday person.
note: 'Las Mañanitas' is the birthday song; on big birthdays, families may hire mariachis to sing it at dawn.

text: A girl's 15th birthday is celebrated like a wedding, with a ball gown and a waltz.
note: The 'quinceañera' has 'chambelanes' (escorts) and a rehearsed waltz. Brazil's 'festa de 15 anos' is similar.

text: At kids' parties, everyone sings while the birthday child swings at a hanging figure full of sweets.
note: The piñata song 'Dale, dale, dale' counts the swings. Today's piñatas are often cartoon characters, not just stars.

text: When a child loses a tooth, a little mouse leaves money under the pillow.
note: Spanish speakers have 'el Ratón Pérez', the French 'la petite souris' and Italians the 'topolino dei denti'; the Tooth Fairy is the English version.

text: Friends compete in duels of double meanings, and getting caught out by one counts as losing.
note: 'Albures' are wordplay battles full of cheeky double meanings; quick replies are admired and slow ones get laughed at.

text: In early November, people write funny rhymes imagining Death coming for their friends.
note: 'Calaveritas literarias' are joking verses about a friend or boss as a skeleton; schools and newspapers publish them.

text: Strangers walking past your table say "enjoy your meal".
note: '¡Provecho!' is ordinary courtesy, even in a restaurant or the office kitchen; reply with 'gracias'.

text: A 1970s TV show about a poor kid living in a barrel is still quoted by all ages.
note: 'El Chavo del Ocho' ran in reruns for decades across Latin America; in Brazil he's 'Chaves' and just as loved.

text: Friends call each other "dude" several times per sentence, using a word that once meant "ox".
note: 'Güey' (or 'wey') started as an insult, 'dumb ox'; now it's friendly filler: '¿Qué onda, güey?'

text: Answering the phone, people say "good?" instead of "hello".
note: '¿Bueno?' may come from early phone lines, when callers checked that the connection was good.

text: To ask someone to repeat, people politely say "command me?".
note: '¿Mande?' means 'pardon?'. It sounds old-fashioned and very courteous to other Spanish speakers.

text: Shouting "waters!" means "watch out!".
note: '¡Aguas!' is said to come from the days when people threw dirty water out of windows with a warning shout.

text: Something cool is described as "how father!".
note: '¡Qué padre!' means 'how cool!', while 'qué mala onda' (what a bad wave) means 'not cool'.

text: Colleagues with a degree are called "Engineer" or "Graduate" instead of by name.
note: Degrees become titles: 'Licenciado' and 'Ingeniero' in Mexico, 'Dottore' and 'Ingegnere' in Italy, even for people you've known for years.

text: By law, every worker gets a December bonus of at least 15 days' pay.
note: The 'aguinaldo' must be paid by 20 December. Brazil goes further with a full '13th salary'.

text: Business emails end with "I remain at your orders", even between equals.
note: 'Quedo a sus órdenes' is a standard polite closing in emails and calls, not a sign of rank.

text: Payday comes twice a month, and shops and traffic peak around the 15th and 30th.
note: Pay arrives every 'quincena' (fortnight), so people plan their spending around it.

text: Meetings open with a warm personal chat; diving straight into business feels cold.
note: Asking about family and the weekend first builds trust (Mexican 'confianza'), which matters more than speed; in Türkiye it comes with a glass of tea.

text: On 28 December people play pranks, and anything you lend that day you may never get back.
note: On 'Día de los Inocentes' the victim hears 'inocente palomita' (innocent little dove), and newspapers print fake stories.

text: The stretch from mid-December to 6 January is jokingly called a party marathon.
note: The 'Guadalupe-Reyes' runs from 12 December to 6 January, one celebration after another.

text: A posh, preppy person is called a "strawberry".
note: A 'fresa' supposedly mixes English words into every sentence and speaks with a sing-song accent.

text: A stingy friend is called an "elbow".
note: 'Codo', often with a tap on your own elbow as the gesture.

text: Get up from your seat and it's gone, and someone recites a rhyme to prove it's fair.
note: 'El que se fue a la Villa perdió su silla' (who went away lost their chair) is the playground and office rule.

text: To hint that a guest has overstayed, people say house guests "start to smell after three days".
note: The full saying: 'el muerto y el arrimado a los tres días apestan' (the dead and the freeloader both stink after three days).

text: A 9-to-5 office worker with a packed lunch and a badge has a teasing nickname.
note: 'Godín', from the surname Godínez; the Spanish Royal Academy recognised the word in 2018.

text: A colleague who flatters the boss is called "the barber".
note: 'Barbero', from 'hacerle la barba' (to trim someone's beard); in Spain it would just mean a barber.

text: "Job" has its own slang word, and "to work" is built from it.
note: 'Chamba' means job and 'chambear' to work; a popular story links it to a US chamber of commerce, but that's disputed.

text: Online orders and bills are often paid in cash at the corner convenience store, using a barcode.
note: You pick the store at checkout, get a voucher and pay the cashier; it serves the many adults without a bank card.

text: At dusk, a steam whistle shrieks down the street: a cart selling baked sweet potatoes.
note: The 'carrito de camotes' has a wood oven whose steam pipe whistles; it also sells plantains with condensed milk.

text: When a bell clangs in the street, neighbours run out with their rubbish bags to catch the truck.
note: The rubbish crew rings a hand bell, and independent collectors shout '¿Quiere basuraaa?' and work for tips.

text: "What's up?" is literally "what wave?"
note: '¿Qué onda?' A bad vibe is 'mala onda' (a bad wave).

text: "No way!" is said as "don't stain!"
note: '¡No manches!' is the polite version of a much ruder phrase.

text: There's an everyday word for a warm, soul-deep hug, borrowed from an Indigenous language.
note: 'Apapachar' comes from Nahuatl and is often explained as 'to embrace with the soul'.

text: "Money talks" becomes "with money, the dog dances".
note: 'Con dinero baila el perro.'

text: Grown-ups call their parents "the boss" and "the lady boss".
note: 'Mi jefe' and 'mi jefa' mean dad and mum; 'mis jefes' are your parents.

text: Mother's Day is 10 May, whatever day of the week it falls on.
note: 'Día de las Madres' never moves to a Sunday; families gather, sing and give gifts, and many schools put on shows.

text: At weddings, the couple stands on chairs while a human chain of guests tries to knock them off.
note: In 'La víbora de la mar' (the sea snake), family members hold the couple up, a symbol of support through life.

text: Serenading someone late at night under their window with hired musicians is "bringing the rooster".
note: 'Llevar gallo' is a night serenade, often with mariachis, for a sweetheart or for mum.

text: Friends or coworkers each put in money every month, and one member takes the whole pot each round.
note: Tanda in Mexico, 'altın günü' (gold day) in Türkiye, 'gye' in Korea: interest-free savings circles built on trust, not paperwork.

text: Once a week, your car has to stay home depending on the last digit of its plate.
note: Mexico City's 'Hoy No Circula' (since 1989) bans vehicles by plate digit and emissions sticker; some cars are exempt, and the capital is its main user.

note: Mexican '¿a poco?' works as 'no way!', 'seriously?' or 'you don't say'.
